headline: Pilbara Minerals slides 3.5% as lithium woes deepen, while Iran war tensions rattle global markets and gold hits fresh highs.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: PLS had a rough session today, dropping 3.5% to $4.76. Lithium prices remain under pressure globally, with news flow around sector peers like Elevra Lithium highlighting how weak spot prices are squeezing the expansion outlook across the industry. The long-term lithium demand story (EVs, batteries) is intact, but the market is being patient.

movers.name: Global X AI ETF
movers.note: The AI ETF slipped 1.1% today to $16.18, tracking broader weakness in tech and AI-related stocks on the ASX. News flow today noted fintech, leveraged ETFs and AI stocks were among the harder-hit segments. This is still down 14.3% from your cost base — a tough one, but the long-term AI growth story hasn't changed.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: VDHG dipped a modest 0.3% today to $77.09, largely reflecting the mild softness across global equities. Nothing specific to worry about here — this is normal daily noise for a diversified fund.

movers.name: Vanguard Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: VGE was essentially flat today, down just 0.14% to $93.11. Emerging markets are dealing with some headwinds from the stronger USD and ongoing global uncertainty around the Iran conflict, but no specific news drove today's tick lower.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market ETF
movers.note: VTS was also near-flat today, down 0.14% to $535.40. The slight dip reflects last night's US market softness (the NASDAQ fell 1.3%), but as a broad US market fund this is everyday noise. The underlying US economy continues to support the long-term case.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: TTWO edged up 0.33% last night to $242.40. There's been a flood of GTA 6 gameplay leak stories this week — hackers released footage as apparent 'retaliation' against Rockstar Games. Despite the drama, the market seems to be taking it in stride. GTA 6 hype, even messy hype, keeps the title in the news cycle.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: MSFT ticked up 0.27% last night to $481.63, continuing to benefit from strong Q2 earnings momentum. Analysts are calling it a standout performer of the recent earnings season, and one Motley Fool piece is modelling MSFT reaching a $5 trillion market cap by 2029 on the back of its AI cloud business. Solid long-term tailwind.

movers.name: Alphabet Inc. (Google)
movers.note: GOOG was essentially unchanged last night, down just 0.05% to $341.28. No specific news catalyst for the holding — the stock is treading water while Microsoft hogged the AI headlines this week. The long-term Google/AI story remains solid.

watch_today.title: Pilbara Minerals (PLS.AX): Lithium pain continues
watch_today.detail: PLS dropped another 3.5% today to $4.76, and you're now sitting at a 29.4% loss on this position. Lithium prices are still soft globally and sector news is broadly negative. The long-term case — EV demand driving lithium demand — is still intact, but this could take years to play out. For a buy-and-hold investor, sit tight rather than crystallise the loss, but don't add here unless you have a genuinely long time horizon and high conviction.

watch_today.title: GXAI.AX: AI ETF down 14% from cost — hold the course
watch_today.detail: GXAI slipped another 1.1% today and is now 14.3% below your cost base. Today's dip was part of a broader AI/tech selloff on the ASX. The underlying AI growth theme is still one of the most powerful long-term trends in markets — this is a case of short-term pain in what should be a multi-year holding. No reason to sell. Hold.

watch_today.title: MSFT: Strong earnings momentum — long-term hold
watch_today.detail: Microsoft nudged up again last night and was flagged as a standout of Q2 earnings season alongside Palantir. With analysts modelling a potential $5 trillion market cap by 2029 driven by AI cloud growth (Azure), this is one of your stronger long-term holdings. Up 8.7% from your cost base. No reason to do anything but sit tight.

watch_today.title: GTA 6 leak drama: watch TTWO this week
watch_today.detail: Hackers released GTA 6 gameplay footage as apparent retaliation against Rockstar Games. The market shrugged it off last night (TTWO +0.33%), but if the leak escalates or causes Rockstar/Take-Two to delay the release, that could weigh on the stock. Keep an eye on it this week. For now, your position is up 4.4% — hold.

watch_today.title: RBA rate hike warning — watch your mortgage and rate-sensitive holdings
watch_today.detail: RBA Deputy Governor Andrew Hauser said today the Bank 'will' raise rates again if inflation doesn't come down — the bluntest warning in months. This keeps pressure on Aussie households with mortgages and could weigh on growth stocks and property. Worth keeping in mind as context for your ASX holdings this week.

watch_today.title: Gold hits $4,409 USD — global uncertainty driving safe-haven demand
watch_today.detail: Gold surged nearly 1% overnight to $4,409/oz, near record highs, as investors seek safety amid the Iran war stalemate and Trump's threats to bomb Oman. You don't hold gold directly, but this signals heightened global risk appetite — a reminder to stay diversified, which your VDHG and VGE positions help with.

world.summary: The Iran-US war remains the dominant global story, with Trump threatening to bomb Oman after 60-day nuclear talks collapse, Iran signalling it could target European military assets, and Gulf oil giants scrambling to secure overseas stockpiles. Gold is surging as investors seek safety.

stories.title: Trump threatens to bomb Oman as Iran nuclear talks collapse
stories.why_it_matters: The 60-day window for US-Iran nuclear negotiations has ended without a deal, and President Trump is now threatening to strike Oman — which had been serving as a diplomatic go-between — if Iran doesn't comply. Trump also confirmed there are no planned further talks with Iran. This is a significant escalation in a conflict that's already been dragging on, and it raises the risk of broader Middle East instability that could impact global energy markets and investor sentiment.

stories.title: Iran eyes military targets in Europe if Trump escalates war
stories.why_it_matters: According to insiders cited by the AFR and the Financial Times, Iran has been privately identifying potential military targets in Europe as a contingency if the US escalates its military campaign. This is a major development — it would represent an unprecedented expansion of the conflict beyond the Middle East. European governments and NATO allies would face enormous pressure to respond, and the geopolitical ripple effects would be felt in every market globally.

stories.title: Gulf oil giants push to expand overseas stockpiles as Iran war drags on
stories.why_it_matters: Saudi Arabia, the UAE and other Gulf oil producers are quietly moving to build up energy stockpiles in overseas locations — a sign they're preparing for the Iran war to intensify or disrupt regional supply chains. This kind of hedging by the world's biggest oil exporters signals the conflict is far from over. For everyday Australians, a prolonged disruption to Middle East oil supply could push petrol prices higher.

stories.title: Asia's economic outlook clouded by global swing factors
stories.why_it_matters: Analysis from The Edge Malaysia highlights that Asia's economic outlook is increasingly uncertain, with the Iran war, slowing Chinese demand, and US trade policy all acting as major headwinds. For Australian investors, this matters because China is our biggest trading partner — anything that slows Asian growth tends to drag on commodity prices (like lithium and iron ore) and the Aussie dollar.

stories.title: US Senator presses Pentagon to keep military out of midterm elections
stories.why_it_matters: US Senator Elissa Slotkin has written to Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth demanding assurances that the US military will not be used for political purposes ahead of the midterm elections. This reflects growing concern in Washington about the blurring of lines between military operations and domestic politics under the current administration — a tension worth watching as the US election cycle heats up.

markets.summary: Last night was a soft session in the US — the NASDAQ fell 1.3% and the S&P 500 dropped 0.7% as Iran war uncertainty and a lack of fresh catalysts weighed on tech stocks. The ASX held up better today, slipping just 0.18%. Gold surged to $4,409/oz on safe-haven demand. The Aussie dollar slipped to US70.8 cents despite the RBA's hawkish tone.

indicators.name: ASX 200
indicators.note: Mild pullback today — held up well relative to US weakness last night.

indicators.name: S&P 500
indicators.note: Last night's session: broad softness driven by Iran war uncertainty and fading risk appetite.

indicators.name: NASDAQ Composite
indicators.note: Last night's session: tech stocks led the selloff, with AI names among the harder-hit segments.

indicators.name: Gold (WTI)
indicators.note: Gold near record highs as investors pile into safe-haven assets amid Iran war escalation.

indicators.name: Crude Oil (WTI)
indicators.note: Oil dipped slightly — surprisingly resilient given the Iran tensions, helped by Gulf nations stockpiling.

indicators.name: AUD/USD
indicators.note: The Aussie dollar fell despite the RBA's hawkish rate warning — global risk-off sentiment and USD strength won out.

politics.summary: The RBA fired its clearest warning yet about more rate hikes, Labor killed off the controversial 'widow tax', gambling reform is set to pass, and a landmark deal on news bargaining laws was struck between Labor and the Coalition.

stories.title: RBA boss fires blunt warning: rates will rise again if inflation doesn't fall
stories.why_it_matters: RBA Deputy Governor Andrew Hauser said in no uncertain terms today that the Reserve Bank 'will have to raise rates again' if inflation doesn't come down — the most direct language the RBA has used in months. Despite this hawkish tone (meaning leaning toward higher rates), the Aussie dollar actually fell, because global risk-off sentiment and a stronger US dollar overpowered the local rate signal. For mortgage holders, this is a clear warning: rate cuts are not on the near-term agenda.

stories.title: Labor kills off 'widow tax' after months of backlash
stories.why_it_matters: The Albanese government has formally abandoned the so-called 'widow tax' — a proposal that would have reduced superannuation death benefits paid to surviving spouses who were financially dependent on their partner. The policy attracted fierce backlash from retirees, women's groups and the crossbench over several months, with critics arguing it disproportionately punished women who had taken time out of work to raise families. Labor's backdown is a significant political retreat.

stories.title: Labor's gambling reform bill set to pass with crossbench support
stories.why_it_matters: Labor's gambling reform legislation — which is expected to include restrictions on online betting advertising and potentially sportsbet promotions — is set to pass parliament, though with some amendments. The bill has been controversial, with the government facing pressure from both the media industry (which relies on gambling advertising revenue) and community health advocates pushing for stricter limits. The passage signals meaningful change to how gambling is marketed in Australia, with effects for broadcasters and online platforms.

stories.title: Labor and Coalition strike deal on news bargaining laws
stories.why_it_matters: The government and Coalition have reached a bipartisan agreement on laws that require digital platforms — primarily Google and Meta — to pay Australian news organisations for using their content. This is an update to the existing News Media Bargaining Code. The deal signals Australia will continue pushing tech giants to fund local journalism, which has broader implications for how news organisations are funded and whether platforms like Google News might change their operations in Australia.

ai.summary: Today's AI news is dominated by regulatory themes — from the FDA being pushed to clarify rules around medical imaging AI, to the broader challenge of biotech AI outpacing the laws meant to govern it. A Chinese AI firm is also making moves in the cybersecurity space.

stories.title: Radiology Partners petitions FDA for clearer rules on medical imaging AI
stories.why_it_matters: Radiology Partners' AI division Mosaic has filed a formal petition with the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) asking for clearer regulatory guidelines around AI tools used in medical imaging — things like AI that reads X-rays, MRIs and CT scans to help diagnose disease. Currently the rules are murky, which makes it hard for hospitals and companies to know what's approved and what's not. Clearer FDA rules would accelerate the adoption of AI diagnostics in healthcare globally, which is one of the most promising near-term applications of the technology.

stories.title: AI in biotech is moving faster than the laws governing it
stories.why_it_matters: A piece in The Conversation highlights a fundamental problem: AI is being adopted in biotechnology — drug discovery, genetic analysis, clinical trials — far faster than regulators can write the rules to govern it. This creates real risks around safety, accountability and data privacy. The same gap exists in Australia, where the TGA (Therapeutic Goods Administration) is still catching up to the pace of AI-driven medical innovation. For investors in AI or biotech, regulatory lag is both a risk and, eventually, a catalyst when rules are finally set.

stories.title: Chinese AI firm Zhipu launches cybersecurity tool in response to US 'Project Glasswing'
stories.why_it_matters: Chinese AI startup Zhipu AI has launched a cybersecurity product it's positioning as a direct counter to the US government's 'Project Glasswing' — an AI-driven cyber defence initiative. This is a visible sign of the US-China AI arms race moving into the cybersecurity domain. As both superpowers race to build AI-powered offensive and defensive cyber tools, the risks of state-sponsored cyberattacks on businesses and governments globally are rising — something Australian companies and government agencies are increasingly having to plan for.

sport.summary: NRL Round 25 is shaping up with team lists confirmed across the competition. The Storm have been busy in the transfer market, locking in a surprise signing for 2027 and poaching a key forward from a Sydney rival. In AFL, a major sponsor has taken action against Sydney Swans stars Isaac Heeney and Chad Warner amid an unfolding club scandal.

stories.title: NRL Round 25 team lists confirmed — Storm, Panthers headline Thursday night
stories.why_it_matters: Team lists are locked in for NRL Round 25. The marquee game is Storm vs Panthers at AAMI Park on Thursday night — a top-of-table clash that could have big finals implications. Locally for Gold Coast fans, the Titans host the Sharks on Sunday at Cbus Super Stadium at 2pm. The Cowboys have the bye this round.

stories.title: Melbourne Storm poach key forward from Sydney rival, lock in surprise 2027 signing
stories.why_it_matters: Melbourne Storm have been active in the transfer market, reportedly poaching a key forward from a Sydney rival ahead of the 2027 season, while also locking in an unexpected signing — details of both deals emerged this week. The Storm continue to build depth ahead of what's shaping up as a strong finals campaign. No specific names were confirmed in available reporting.

stories.title: AFL: Major sponsor acts against Heeney and Warner amid Sydney Swans scandal
stories.why_it_matters: A major sponsor of the Sydney Swans has taken action against star forwards Isaac Heeney and Chad Warner following an unfolding club scandal. Details of the specific sponsor action and the nature of the scandal were not fully detailed in available reporting, but the involvement of sponsors signals the controversy has moved beyond a purely on-field or internal matter, with commercial consequences now in play. A significant story to follow.

stories.title: AFL Gather Round 2027 dates locked in — biggest yet
stories.why_it_matters: The AFL has officially locked in dates for the 2027 Gather Round — the league's festival-of-football concept where all 18 clubs play in one city over a long weekend. The 2027 edition is set to be the biggest yet, expanding the concept further. Gather Round has been a big commercial and fan success since its Adelaide debut, and its growth reflects the AFL's confidence in the format as a marquee annual event.
